The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

For $a>0$, define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. The operator norm below is induced by the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for finite $R\ge0$, $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ is continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$. For $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the probability measure

$$\nu_{t,x}(dz)=\frac{\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mu(dz),\qquad m_{t,x}=\int z\,\nu_{t,x}(dz),$$

and the matrix

$$C_{t,x}=\int (z-m_{t,x})(z-m_{t,x})^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{t,x}(dz).$$

The density $p_t$ is positive and smooth, and its score $s_t(x):=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ satisfies

$$s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_{t,x}}{v(t)},\qquad D_xs_t(x)=-\frac{I_d}{v(t)}+\frac{C_{t,x}}{v(t)^2}.$$

For all $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|D_xs_t(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac1{v(\epsilon)}+\frac{R^2}{v(\epsilon)^2},\qquad |s_t(x)|\le\frac{|x|+R}{v(\epsilon)},$$

so $s_t$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$, uniformly over this truncated time interval, with Lipschitz constant at most $1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2$. No such bound is asserted uniformly as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$, a compactly supported Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, a continuously differentiable function $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ bounded above and away from zero, and $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2dr$. For $t>0$ put
$$p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(y-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x)\quad(0\le s<t\le T),$$
where $\phi_a$ is the centered Gaussian density with covariance $aI_d$. Put $p_0=\mu$ as a probability measure, not as a Lebesgue density. For $0\le u<v<T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\,dx,$$
and for $0\le u<T$ at the singular data endpoint define
$$K_{u,T}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A q(0,x;T-u,y)\,\mu(dx)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\quad(A\text{ Borel}).$$
Set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. These are the Bayes-reversed kernels of the additive Gaussian smoothing process, including the posterior kernel at the original data time; no density for $\mu$ is required.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The Gaussian forward process is Markov by independent increments of its deterministic Itô integral. Bayes' formula gives the reversed conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$ as $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$; the density supplier's marginal identity normalizes it, and [F3] gives reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov. Thus $Y$ is Markov with these kernels.

Put $t=T-u$ and $\delta v=v(t)-v(t-h)$ for $h>0$. For $u+h\le T-\epsilon$, the reverse transition formula gives $\displaystyle K_{u,u+h}\varphi(y)=\frac{1}{p_t(y)}\int \varphi(x)p_{t-h}(x)\phi_{\delta v}(y-x)\,dx.$ The heat-kernel expansion, justified on the compact support of $\varphi$ by [F1, F4], is $\displaystyle \int \varphi(x)p_{t-h}(x)\phi_{\delta v}(y-x)dx=p_t(y)\varphi(y)+\frac{\delta v}{2}\left(\Delta(p_t\varphi)(y)-\varphi(y)\Delta p_t(y)\right)+o(\delta v).$ Since $\delta v/h\to g(t)^2$, the product rule gives $\displaystyle \lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{K_{u,u+h}\varphi(y)-\varphi(y)}h=g(t)^2\left(\nabla\log p_t(y)\cdot\nabla\varphi(y)+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi(y)\right)=\widetilde L_u\varphi(y).$ The remainder is locally uniform in $y$ and dominated on the compact test support because $t\ge\epsilon$.

Fix $u$, put $b=T-u$, and write $P_cf=\phi_c*f$. For $r>u$, put $a=T-r$. The explicit kernel gives $K_{u,r}\varphi(y)=P_{v(b)-v(a)}(p_a\varphi)(y)/p_b(y)$. Differentiate in $r$, using the heat equation and integrating the Gaussian Laplacian onto the compactly supported function $p_a\varphi$, to obtain $\displaystyle \partial_rK_{u,r}\varphi(y)=\frac{g(a)^2}{2p_b(y)}P_{v(b)-v(a)}\!\left(\Delta(p_a\varphi)-\varphi\Delta p_a\right)(y)=K_{u,r}(\widetilde L_r\varphi)(y).$ Away from $r=u$, differentiation is justified by [F4]: the variance is positive, the spatial support is fixed compact, and $p_a,\partial_a p_a$ and the needed state derivatives are uniformly bounded there for $a\ge\epsilon$. The product rule gives the last equality. By [F2], $|\widetilde L_r\varphi(x)|\le C$ uniformly in $x,r$ on the truncated interval, so the probability-kernel property bounds the derivative by $C$. Integrate from $u+\delta$ to $v$ and let $\delta\downarrow0$: step 1.2 gives $K_{u,u+\delta}\varphi(y)\to\varphi(y)$, while the bound $C$ controls the omitted integral. Thus $K_{u,v}\varphi-\varphi=\int_u^vK_{u,r}(\widetilde L_r\varphi)dr$. For $s<v$, Markovness and bounded conditional Fubini give $\displaystyle E\!\left[\varphi(Y_v)-\varphi(Y_s)-\int_s^v\widetilde L_r\varphi(Y_r)dr\mid\mathcal G_s\right]=K_{s,v}\varphi(Y_s)-\varphi(Y_s)-\int_s^vK_{s,r}(\widetilde L_r\varphi)(Y_s)dr=0.$ This proves the martingale claim.

boundaries.evidence: At v=0 the displayed compensated process is phi(Y0)-phi(Y0) minus an integral over the empty time interval, hence zero. A zero test also gives the identically zero martingale; neither case needs a score at the excluded forward time 0. The Statement displays the compensated process for 0<=v<=T-epsilon. Proof step 2.1 proves its martingale property; substituting v=0 in that displayed process gives the stated zero value, and its compact-test argument also permits the zero test.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all three current proof steps and full Gaussian density and score suppliers. Bayes normalization gives reversed Markovness. The small-time heat expansion is locally uniform for fixed positive forward time, but the martingale proof does not integrate that remainder. Instead the exact target-time derivative of P_(v(b)-v(a))(p_a phi)/p_b is K_(u,r)(Ltilde_r phi), by the heat equation and compact-support integration by parts. The test generator has a uniform global bound on forward times >=epsilon; probability normalization bounds the derivative by that same constant. Integrating away from the diagonal then using the approximate identity limit proves the finite-time identity. Bounded conditional Fubini gives the true martingale. This independently confirms the earlier local repair ml101-b67-gaussian-kernel-integrated-identity. Singular mu and R=0 are allowed; no score at zero or unproved generic generator inference remains.
